ta-l1d17q2-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus for the second part of Distinction 17, where Lombard raises objections to his thesis. If charity is the Spirit and charity increases and decreases in a person, must one grant that the Spirit increases and decreases? He answers that the Spirit, or charity, is wholly immutable, and confirms this by authority. He then faces three arguments from authorities: the love by which we love God differs from the love by which God loves us, which is the Spirit; charity is said to be from God, like faith, which is not God; and charity is called an affection or movement of the mind, which the Spirit is not. Five articles are announced: whether charity increases, how, whether by any act whatever, whether its increase has a limit, and whether it decreases.
claims: Lombard answers objections to his identification of charity with the Spirit by appeal to the Spirit's immutability.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3531.summary: First argument that charity does not increase. Only what has quantity increases, and nothing simple is quantified, since every quantity is divisible. Charity is a simple habit and not quantified per se, nor per accidens, since its subject, the soul, is indivisible.
claims: Only quantities increase, and charity and the soul are simple.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3534.summary: Anticipates the reply that charity has a quantity of power, not of bulk. The quantity of a power is divided by the objects it can reach, and any charity, however small, reaches all objects of charity.
claims: Quantity of power is measured by the number of objects.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3537.summary: Second argument. Increase is a species of motion, so what increases is moved, and what increases essentially is moved essentially. What is moved is a body (the Philosopher), and what is naturally moved is corrupted. Charity is not corrupted ('charity never fails', 1 Cor. 13:8) and is not a movable body.
claims: What is moved is a body and is corruptible.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3544.summary: Third argument. What has a cause that always stands the same neither increases nor decreases, and charity's immediate cause is God, who always stands the same.
claims: An invariable cause produces an invariable effect.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3547.summary: Fourth argument. Increase of a quality can be reduced only to alteration, and alteration concerns only the sensitive part of the soul and its objects (the Philosopher). Charity is a quality in the intellective part, otherwise it would not be in angels, who lack the sensitive part.
claims: Alteration concerns only the sensitive part.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3550.summary: Sed contra from Augustine: charity, once born, is nourished, and once strengthened, is perfected. Whatever progresses through different degrees increases.
claims: Charity progresses through degrees.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3556.summary: Second sed contra. We know habits through acts, and an act of charity can become more intense, so charity can increase.
claims: Acts of charity can intensify.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3559.summary: Thomas's determination. Some held that charity does not increase essentially, in four ways. (1) Lombard holds that charity does not increase in itself but is said to increase in us as we advance in it, since he takes charity to be the Spirit, who cannot vary. But advancing in the Spirit is unintelligible without something new in us, and that cannot be only an act, since every act comes from a power and a perfect act from a power perfected by a habit. (2) Some say charity is said to increase as it is more firmly rooted in its subject. But a form is more firmly rooted only by greater mastery over its subject, which means greater power and so greater essence, since power comes from essence and is commensurate with it. (3) Some say that when greater charity comes, the lesser is destroyed. But a form is destroyed only by a contrary agent or accidentally by the subject's corruption, and neither applies. (4) Some say charity increases only in fervour. Fervour taken metaphorically, as the intensity of the act of charity, follows charity's essence per se, so it cannot increase unless charity does. Fervour as in the sensitive part, the impression that the higher affection's motion toward God leaves in the sensitive powers, does not measure merit, since it depends on bodily disposition, so the more fervent do not always merit more. So charity increases essentially. To increase is to take on greater quantity. Virtual quantity is not quantity by genus and is not divided by division of its essence; its magnitude is measured by something external that is divisible or multipliable, its object or act. By genus it is an accidental form in quality or a substantial form, which does not admit more and less. So increase in virtual quantity belongs not to the motion called increase but to alteration, and in this way charity and other qualities increase. Dimensive quantity belongs to some things per accidens, like whiteness through surface, and per se to bodies. Thomas distinguishes increase by addition without motion (wood added to wood), true motion of increase in which quantity is the per se terminus and every part grows (only in things with a nutritive power), and quantity following a form, which is generation or alteration rather than increase.
claims: Charity increases essentially, against Lombard and others.
Lombard's view fails because progress in charity requires a new perfecting habit in us.
Charity increases in virtual quantity, by alteration, not by the motion of growth.
Bodily fervour does not measure merit.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3562.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although charity has no dimensive quantity, per se or per accidens, since its subject has none, it has a quantity of power by reason of which it is said to increase, like whiteness and heat.
claims: Charity increases in quantity of power.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3566.summary: Reply to the second argument. Quantity of power is measured in two ways: by the number of objects, like discrete quantity, and by the intensity of the act on the same object, like continuous quantity. It is in the latter way that charity's power grows.
claims: Charity grows in intensity of act on the same object, not in number of objects.
concepts: discrete vs. continuous quantity of power

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3569.summary: Reply to the third argument. Charity is said to increase not as the subject of increase, since it is an accident, but because increase is measured by it, as quantity is said to increase and whiteness to vary when something varies by whiteness. Essential increase need not mean destruction. Something is said to be moved in its essence when its essence is the per se terminus of motion, which is losing the essence and being corrupted, or when something joined to the essence is the per se terminus, as a thing moved in place is moved essentially because it is in place by its essence. So essential increase is by a quantity following the essence, while the essence remains one under diverse quantity, whether that quantity is the essence itself, as quantity of power is identical with the power, or something else, as in bodily growth. Not everything moved is a body, except in natural motion, which the soul's motion is not.
claims: Essential increase keeps the essence the same under different quantity.
Not all motion is bodily.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3572.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Although charity's efficient cause is immobile in itself, by the order of his wisdom he can give someone greater charity at the pleasure of his will, and according as someone prepares for charity in different ways. The recipient relates to charity somewhat as a receiving material cause, and its diversity varies the effect.
claims: Variation in charity comes from God's free ordering and the recipient's diverse preparation.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3575.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Since passive alteration includes passion, and passion is twofold, so is alteration. In a common sense, passion is any reception, as understanding is a kind of undergoing, and alteration in this sense is any variation in receiving a quality, which can be even in purely intellectual substances and in charity. In the proper sense, passion is when something is removed from a substance by the action of a contrary, and alteration so taken concerns only sensibles and the sensitive part per se, and the intellect per accidens as to qualities arising in it from the senses, such as all acquired habits, of which charity is not one.
claims: Charity increases by alteration in the broad sense of variation in reception.
concepts: two senses of passio and alteratio

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3587.summary: First argument that charity increases by addition. The Philosopher says increase is an addition to a pre-existing quantity, so another charity must be added to the existing one.
claims: Increase is addition to a pre-existing quantity.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3593.summary: Second argument. Only God, who gave charity, can increase it, and God does nothing new in the soul except by a new influx, which means something newly infused, so another charity is infused and added.
claims: A new divine influx implies something newly infused.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3596.summary: Third argument. If charity is not increased by God's adding new charity, it can only increase by withdrawal from its contrary. But charity can increase where there is nothing contrary to it, as in angels and in humans in innocence, so it increases by addition.
claims: Charity increases even without a contrary.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3600.summary: Fourth argument. On the alternative view, the cause of charity's increase would be not God but the person restraining themselves from what is contrary to charity, such as concupiscence, which is unfitting.
claims: Increase by removing contraries would make humans the cause.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3603.summary: Sed contra. Something simple added to something simple makes nothing greater (the Philosopher), and charity is simple.
claims: Simple added to simple makes nothing greater.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3606.summary: Second sed contra from Dionysius: participations of God are nobler the simpler they are, while participants are nobler the more participated gifts they combine, as being is nobler than living and living than understanding taken singly, but having more of them is better. Charity is a participation of divine goodness, so the more composite it became by addition, the less it would be worth, which is absurd.
claims: Participations are nobler the simpler they are.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3609.summary: Thomas's determination. Those who hold that charity increases essentially have two views: by addition of charity to charity, or by intensification through approach to a terminus, which is what some mean by charity multiplying itself in the soul like light in air. Thomas cannot understand the first, since addition requires two distinct things. Two charities would differ in species or number, not in species, since all charity is one species, and numerical diversity comes from diversity of matter, as this whiteness differs from that because it is in another subject. Charity added never existed in another subject, and in this subject it does not differ numerically from the charity already there. The view comes from imagining charity's growth like bodily growth by addition of quantity to quantity. So when charity increases nothing is added; as the Philosopher says, something becomes whiter or hotter not by addition of whiteness or heat but because the quality already present is intensified by nearness to its terminus. Composite or secondary qualities intensify by the intensification of the primary ones. Simple primary qualities intensify from their causes, agent and recipient. The agent tends to bring the patient from potency to act in its likeness as much as it can, and as the not-hot is in potency to heat, the less hot is in potency to the hotter, so the heat already present as imperfect act is brought to greater perfection and likeness to the agent. This happens as the potency, which of itself is open to many, is more and more determined by that act, either because the agent's power grows, as light intensifies with more lamps, or because the matter becomes more receptive, as air becomes more receptive of light the more it is rarefied. Charity's intensification comes not from strengthening of the agent's power but only from the receiving nature being more and more prepared, gathered into one out of the confusion of its potentiality by the operations preparing it for charity. Hence Dionysius describes the perfection of holiness as rising from scattered life into unity. So charity's increase is like that of natural qualities, though its origin differs. Natural qualities are educed from the potency of matter, in which God placed their beginnings at creation. Gratuitous gifts are not educed from natural potency, since nothing in natural potency cannot be educed by a natural agent, so grace originates by new infusion, and its increase is the bringing of the infused act from imperfect to perfect.
claims: Charity does not increase by addition, since two charities in one subject are unintelligible.
Charity increases by intensification, as the infused act is brought from imperfect to perfect.
Charity's intensification comes from the recipient's preparation, as its potentiality is gathered into unity, not from strengthening of the divine agent.
Grace originates by new infusion and grows by intensification.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3612.summary: Reply to the first argument. The Philosopher's proposition concerns bodily increase, which always happens by addition of quantity, since that is the subject he is treating.
claims: Increase by addition applies to bodies.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3615.summary: Reply to the second argument. God acts in all that exists by one and the same operation, though it may differ conceptually as proceeding under different attributes or ideas. So grace is infused and increased by one and the same operation, the diversity being only on the recipient's side, which receives more or less from that operation as it is prepared, as the same sunlight makes the air clear and clearer once cloudy vapours are dispelled, without another clarity. Even if there were two operations, they need not terminate in two substantially different things: the first would terminate in imperfect charity, the second in the same charity perfected.
claims: God infuses and increases grace by one operation; diversity lies in the recipient's preparation.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3619.summary: Reply to the third argument. It does not belong to the concept of a quality's intensification that it come from removal of a contrary; that is incidental, when the quality is in a subject that shares the contrary. What is necessary is that the quality be brought from imperfect to perfect, as light can intensify in a transparent medium with no contrary when the illuminating power grows. This imperfection comes from the potentiality of the nature subject to perfection and act. Every receptive potency is open to many and in this multiplicity is unlike the active principle, which is determined to one act; the more this confusion of potentiality is subjected to act, the more perfect the act and the more one and like the agent it becomes. This confusion of potentiality is in every created nature not yet perfected by act, which is how Dionysius speaks of purgation in angels, as removal from the confusion of unlikeness.
claims: Intensification is bringing a quality from imperfect to perfect, not essentially removing a contrary.
Created potency's multiplicity is unified by act, as in angelic purgation.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3622.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. We are the cause of the increase of grace in the same way as of grace itself, only by way of disposition; efficiency in both cases is God's.
claims: We cause grace and its increase only dispositively; God is the efficient cause.
concepts: God as efficient cause of grace

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3634.summary: First argument that charity increases with every act. Where the cause is the same the effect is the same, and all acts of charity are of the same moral species, so if one increases charity every one does.
claims: Same cause, same effect.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3637.summary: Second argument. What can do the greater can do the lesser. By any act of charity one merits eternal life, so one can merit an increase of charity.
claims: Any act of charity merits eternal life.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3640.summary: Third argument. Any act of charity is far more powerful in the order of grace than acts from natural endowments alone, which dispose a person to receive grace, so any act of charity disposes all the more to its increase.
claims: Acts of charity are stronger than natural acts that dispose to grace.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3644.summary: Sed contra. A thing grows from the same principles from which it is born. One act does not suffice to dispose for the infusion of charity, since our acts have more causality toward acquired virtue than toward infused charity, and one act does not suffice to generate acquired virtue: one becomes good by acting well often (the Philosopher). So neither does one act suffice for its increase.
claims: One act does not generate an acquired virtue.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3647.summary: Second sed contra. As charity increases, the substantial reward increases, and it is commonly said that doing many works in charity does not merit more substantial reward than one work done from equal charity. So not every act increases charity.
claims: Many works from equal charity merit no more substantial reward than one.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3650.summary: Thomas's determination. An act informed by charity relates to its increase differently from an act preceding charity relates to having it. An act from charity is ordered to its increase both as disposition and as merit; an act preceding charity is ordered to obtaining it only as disposition, since there is no merit before charity. Neither is ordered to having or increasing charity by efficiency, as our acts are to acquired habits. Sometimes one act preceding charity disposes with the final disposition for charity to be infused, given the constancy of divine goodness, which gives to each as it is prepared; sometimes one act disposes only remotely, and later acts dispose more, until the final disposition is reached, each later act acting by the power of all the earlier ones, as drops hollow a stone. This is because a person is master of their act and can act with all or part of the power of their nature, unlike things that act by natural necessity, which always act with all their power. When someone without charity is moved toward charity with the whole power of their natural goodness, one act disposes them finally; when only partly, the act is a remote disposition and they may reach the final disposition through several acts. Likewise, when an act of charity proceeds from the whole power of the one who has it, both of nature and of the infused habit, one act disposes for and merits an increase, which follows at once. When it does not proceed from the whole power, it is a remote disposition, and several acts may lead to the increase, though not necessarily, since a person, however disposed, can fail to act according to that disposition, unlike involuntary dispositions.
claims: An act of charity disposes for and merits charity's increase; acts before charity only dispose.
An act from one's whole power suffices for immediate increase; lesser acts are remote dispositions that accumulate.
Free agents can act with all or part of their power, so not every act increases charity.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3653.summary: Reply to the first argument. Not every act of charity is alike: one can be more intense, and one can dispose by the power of several earlier acts, so the same effect does not follow.
claims: Acts of charity differ in intensity and cumulative power.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3656.summary: Reply to the second argument. The substantial reward of eternal life is ordered to acts of charity as their end and is commensurate with them not by equality but by proportion, so an act of charity deserves the substantial reward and an act of greater charity a greater reward. Every act of charity, as informed by the habit, is ordered to the substantial reward, but not to its increase or to the increase of charity, while charity remains the first principle of merit, except insofar as charity's increase belongs to the perfection of the reward.
claims: Every act of charity merits eternal life proportionally, but not every act merits an increase.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3659.summary: Reply to the third argument. An act of charity exceeds an act preceding charity in having the power of meriting, so it comes closer to the causality of charity.
claims: Acts of charity have merit, unlike acts preceding charity.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3663.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Two things are required to introduce a perfection. On the side of the one introducing it, its operation must equal the perfection to be introduced, as fire's heat is introduced not by a small heating but by one with power equal, at least in its principle, to fire's heat. On the side of the recipient, its disposition must be proportioned to the perfection. In the soul's works something sometimes disposes itself and receives perfection from itself, as in science and virtue, so for a perfect disposition it suffices that the soul act with power proportioned to the perfection to be introduced. Since the whole capacity of the soul barely suffices to receive so great a perfection as charity unless God supplies it from his liberality, the final disposition for charity requires an act from the soul's whole power, which suffices on our part, and less does not. Further, where the soul's act produces not only the disposition but the perfection itself, its act must equal the perfection in power. Every habit is by its concept hard to remove, having a kind of firmness, so when one act of the soul has firmness it produces a habit, as one demonstration, by its certainty, produces science. When one act lacks firmness, several are needed, as one dialectical argument does not produce opinion. Since the human will is indeterminate toward many things, its acts lack firmness, so political virtues acquired by acts of will require many acts. The habit of charity has its firmness not from the soul's act but from its cause, God, so one act of will can suffice for charity to be infused and likewise increased.
claims: One act from the soul's whole power suffices as final disposition for charity or its increase.
A habit requires firmness: one demonstration produces science, but political virtues need many acts.
Charity has its firmness from God, not from our acts, so one act can suffice for it.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3666.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. When an act of charity is such as is required for charity's increase, the substantial reward also increases, due to the greater charity following the act, not to the charity that is the root of the act. Not all acts are such, so many acts do not necessarily increase the substantial reward.
claims: Only acts that increase charity increase the substantial reward.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3679.summary: First argument that charity's increase has a limit. A perfection does not exceed the capacity of the perfectible, and the soul's capacity is finite, so it can receive only finite perfection, and every motion toward a finite terminus is finite.
claims: The soul's capacity is finite.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3682.summary: Second argument. Nothing moves in an orderly way toward what it cannot reach (the Philosopher), and no one can reach what is infinitely distant, since no motion spans an infinite distance. So no motion is infinite, and the increase of charity, a motion, reaches a terminus.
claims: No motion spans an infinite distance.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3685.summary: Third argument. Lombard says even God cannot make anything greater than Christ's grace (Book III, Dist. 13). If charity's increase were infinite, there could always be a greater charity. Similarly Anselm says the Virgin shone with a purity than which no greater can be conceived under God, and the blessed's charity cannot increase. So charity's increase reaches a limit.
claims: Christ's grace, the Virgin's purity, and the blessed's charity cannot increase.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3689.summary: Sed contra. Charity increases by greater likeness to God, and however close one comes to God's likeness, one remains infinitely distant, so one can always come closer.
claims: One always remains infinitely distant from God's likeness.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3692.summary: Second sed contra. An act of charity from greater charity has more power to merit. If an act of imperfect charity merits an increase, an act of more perfect charity merits it all the more, so charity's increase never stops.
claims: Greater charity merits more increase.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3695.summary: Thomas's determination. The limit of charity's increase can be discussed as to what is or as to what can be, as there is a worst evil than which nothing is worse, though none than which nothing could be worse. So in every person charity's increase reaches a limit beyond which it does not in fact increase, but not one beyond which it could not increase. The reason lies in both terms of the motion. That to which the soul moves is likeness to divine charity, which, being infinite, can be approached more and more without ever being perfectly equalled. On the side of what is moved, the more the soul receives of divine goodness and the light of grace, the more capable it becomes of receiving, so the more it receives the more it can receive. Material powers are limited by their matter and receive only in proportion to it, but immaterial powers are not limited by matter but rather by the quantity of divine goodness received in them, so the more goodness is added, the more potency there is for capacity, as the Philosopher notes that strong sensibles destroy the senses while the intellect, the more it understands difficult things, the more it can. Some, comparing spiritual to material capacity, said charity's increase is limited by the capacity of nature: once the original natural capacity is filled, no more can be received, as air has a limit of subtlety beyond which it cannot be purified or illumined further. But spiritual and material capacity are not alike.
claims: In each person charity's increase actually stops at some point, but there is no limit beyond which it could not increase.
Charity tends to infinite divine charity, and the soul's capacity grows with what it receives.
Immaterial powers are enlarged, not exhausted, by what they receive.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3698.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although the soul's capacity is actually finite, it can be extended further and further within the finite as it receives more, though it will never be infinite or receive infinite perfection. Likewise in adding numbers, which is possible to infinity, no number is ever actually infinite, because the potency for adding numbers is not one but becomes another with each new addition, as a new species of number arises (the Commentator). Each potency can be actualized, but not all, since each act adds a new potency, and so too with the soul's capacity.
claims: The soul's capacity grows indefinitely, like the potential infinity of number, without becoming actually infinite.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3701.summary: Reply to the second argument. Every increase of charity has a terminus that a person can reach, but since that terminus is not pure act but mixed with potency, another increase can follow, and so on to infinity. In this sense charity's increase is unlimited.
claims: Each increase is finite, but increase can succeed increase indefinitely.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3704.summary: Reply to the third argument. Christ's grace, though finite in essence, was infinite in a qualified sense, as a disposition fitting for the union and as concurring in the operation of Christ, who had infinite power as a divine person, and in other ways (Book III, Dist. 17), and for this reason it could not increase. As to the Virgin, increase of purity differs from increase of charity. Increase of purity is by withdrawal from the contrary, and since the Virgin was purified of all sin, she reached the summit of purity, under God, in whom there is no potency for failing, as there is in every creature of itself. Increase of charity is by approach to divine goodness, so the Virgin did not have the highest charity than which no greater can be conceived, since she also advanced in charity and grace. As to the blessed, their charity does not increase because of their state, since they are not on the way but at its end, and they are rewarded according to how charity grew in them on the way.
claims: Christ's grace is qualifiedly infinite and so cannot increase.
The Virgin reached the summit of purity but continued to grow in charity.
The blessed do not increase in charity because they are at the end of the way.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3716.summary: First argument that charity decreases. Contraries naturally occur in the same subject, and increase and decrease are contraries, so since charity increases it can decrease.
claims: Contraries occur in the same subject.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3719.summary: Second argument from Augustine: where cupidity is great, charity is small, and he loves you less who loves something with you. Cupidity can increase, so charity can decrease.
claims: Charity and cupidity vary inversely.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3728.summary: Third argument. Venial sin is an evil of fault, and every evil takes away some opposed good, so venial sin takes away some of charity. Not all of it, since that would exclude from the kingdom (only charity divides the sons of the kingdom from those of perdition, Augustine) and make it mortal. So it diminishes charity.
claims: Every evil removes some opposed good.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3732.summary: Fourth argument. God infuses grace according to how one disposes oneself, since divine light is present to all (Augustine) and those who do not receive it turn away, like one closing their eyes to the sun. One may dispose oneself less than before, so one will share less of grace and charity.
claims: Grace is received according to disposition.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3735.summary: Sed contra. Every created charity is finite, and every finite thing is consumed by repeated subtraction (the Philosopher). If one venial sin diminished charity, the next would too, and multiplied venial sins would remove all charity. Charity is removed only by mortal sin, so many venial sins would make one mortal, which no one holds.
claims: Repeated subtraction consumes a finite whole.
Many venial sins do not make a mortal sin.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3738.summary: Anticipates the reply that this subtraction is like dividing a continuum by the same proportion rather than the same quantity, which can go on forever. But when division is by the same proportion, what is later taken is always less than what was taken before, whereas a later venial sin may have no less power than the first, so it would take as much charity, and charity would be consumed.
claims: Later venial sins need not be weaker than earlier ones.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3741.summary: Thomas's determination. Charity cannot diminish essentially, except by succession: the charity present is destroyed by mortal sin and later a lesser charity is infused through lesser preparation. The cause of a decrease cannot lie with God, to whom no defect is traced as its cause, since he is complete act, so it would have to lie with us. Defect on our side comes from cessation of acts or from disorder. Charity is not weakened in itself by cessation of acts, as acquired habits are, since its firmness comes from the inflowing principle, not from our acts, so its strength remains when acts cease. But frequent acts dispose all the soul's powers and bring the body's members into charity's service, in which fervour consists, so idleness cools charity's fervour. Acquired virtues have their strength from our works and weaken in themselves when works cease. Disorder of act concerns either the end, removing it, in which case charity, by which one clings to the end, is removed, which is mortal sin; or the means while the end remains, lingering inordinately over them, which is venial sin and does not touch charity, since charity is clinging to the end, and so diminishes nothing of it. As means dispose to the end, disorder in them disposes to disorder about the end, which is why venial sin is called a disposition to mortal sin, and by venial sins one is disposed to lose charity. So charity is said to diminish in its rootedness and fervour, not in its essence: in rootedness, as a disposition to the contrary arises and charity's firm clinging is weakened; in fervour, as the obedience of the lower powers to the higher, from which fervour came, is impeded.
claims: Charity does not diminish essentially; it is lost only by mortal sin and may be reinfused in lesser degree.
Charity's firmness comes from God, so cessation of acts cools only its fervour.
Venial sin concerns means, not the end, so it does not diminish charity but disposes to its loss.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3744.summary: Reply to the first argument. Contraries naturally occur in the same subject unless one of them is naturally present, which happens when it follows on its causes. Increase can have a cause on the side of both recipient and giver, but decrease cannot.
claims: Charity has causes of increase but none of decrease.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3747.summary: Reply to the second argument. The inverse proportion of cupidity and charity can concern charity's coming to be or its being. As to its coming to be, the more cupidity dominates through disordered acts, the less one is disposed for charity or its increase, since our acts dispose for these. As to its being, since our acts do not cause charity's being, disordered acts from cupidity take nothing from it but only from its fervour, as the lower parts are made unfit to obey charity.
claims: Cupidity hinders the acquisition and fervour of charity, not its being.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3751.summary: Reply to the third argument. Venial sin cannot take anything from charity, since it does not reach the part of the soul where charity is. As the higher part of the intellect considers self-evident principles, through which other things are known, so that no doubt about conclusions lessens the certainty of principles, the higher part of affection clings to the end for whose sake everything is loved. Whatever disorder concerns the means does not lessen clinging to the end through charity unless a contrary end is posited. Venial sin, positing no undue end, does not reach the summit of affection where charity is. As venial sin is not sin simply but as a disposition to mortal sin, it deprives one of the good that functions as a disposition to charity, its fervour, which lies in the readiness of act from the diligent obedience of the lower powers to the higher part of affection.
claims: Venial sin does not reach the summit of affection, where charity clings to the end.
Venial sin removes only fervour, a disposition to charity.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3754.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Disposition to charity lies in the acts of the lower powers as they deal with means, as one reaches the end through means. Once the end is had, the means are not needed, so disorder about them affects the end only by way of disposition, as knowledge of first principles is determined in us through the senses, yet if the senses are destroyed the certainty of principles, which is not acquired but naturally implanted, is not lessened. So too with infused charity.
claims: Once charity is had, disorder in means affects it only dispositively.

ta-l1d17q2-d1e3763.summary: An expositio textus on Lombard's responses. (1) God is called great and exalted in us by making us great and high in himself, which can only be by a fuller perception of his goodness, so one must return to positing something created by God in us. (2) Many do not have the Spirit; only those are said to have him whose inheritance he is, who enjoy him in hope or in reality. (3) 'Without the Spirit we cannot love Christ or keep his commands' is true meritoriously of the Spirit had through charity, and true universally of the Spirit acting in any way, though the latter is not Augustine's meaning. (4) Elisha's request for a double share of Elijah's spirit, though glossed as prophecy and miracles, still shows that the Spirit is had unequally. (5) Each person's 'proper measure' is from God's predestination and from the recipient's natural capacity and effort. (6) Of the authorities against Lombard: he answers the first, that the love by which God loves differs from the love by which we love, by a merely conceptual difference. He answers the second, that charity is from the Spirit, by saying the Spirit gives himself, which is insufficient, since charity is said to be from him, which cannot be said of the Spirit. He answers the third, that charity is a movement of the mind, by causal predication, which is true but not in his sense, since charity causes affection as a habit eliciting an act, not only as moving the soul. His explanation of why the Spirit is said specially to move to the act of love leaves unexplained his assumption that the Spirit causes this act with no habit mediating. (7) Not everyone has every gift: the uncreated gift and the gifts of sanctifying grace, infused together, are common to the saints, but freely given gifts are given more to manifest the Spirit received than to join one to him, for others' benefit (1 Cor. 12), and are divided according to the Church's needs.
claims: God's greatness in us implies something created in us.
Lombard's replies to the authorities are insufficient: charity is from the Spirit and causes love as an eliciting habit.
Gifts of sanctifying grace are common to the saints; freely given graces are distributed for the Church's benefit.
concepts: gratia gratum faciens vs. gratis data

ta-l1d17q2-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of the second part of Distinction 17 sets out Lombard's handling of objections to his identification of charity with the Spirit, from charity's increase and decrease and from authorities, and announces five articles on the increase and decrease of charity.

ta-l1d17q2-Dd1e3523.summary: Article 1 asks whether charity increases. Thomas rejects four views on which it does not increase essentially: Lombard's (we advance in an immutable Spirit), firmer rooting, destruction of lesser by greater charity, and mere fervour. He holds that charity increases essentially, in virtual quantity, measured by intensity of act on the same object, through alteration in the broad sense of variation in reception, not bodily growth. Variation comes from God's ordering and the recipient's preparation.
claims: Charity increases essentially in quantity of power, by alteration.
Lombard's view that only our participation in the Spirit increases is rejected.

ta-l1d17q2-Dd1e3579.summary: Article 2 asks how charity increases. Thomas rejects increase by addition, since two charities in one subject are unintelligible. Charity increases by intensification, as the infused act is brought from imperfect to perfect. This comes not from a strengthened divine agent but from the recipient's preparation, as its scattered potentiality is gathered into unity. Grace originates by infusion rather than eduction, God infuses and increases it by one operation, and we cause its increase only dispositively.
claims: Charity increases by intensification, not addition, through the recipient's preparation.

ta-l1d17q2-Dd1e3626.summary: Article 3 asks whether every act of charity increases it. Acts of charity dispose and merit its increase, while acts before charity only dispose. An act from one's whole power suffices as final disposition for immediate increase, while lesser acts are remote dispositions that may accumulate like drops on a stone, though not necessarily, since free agents can act below their power. Charity's firmness comes from God, so one act can suffice, unlike acquired virtues. Every act of charity merits eternal life proportionally, but only acts that increase charity increase the substantial reward.
claims: Not every act of charity increases it; one act from one's whole power suffices.
Every act of charity merits eternal life.

ta-l1d17q2-Dd1e3671.summary: Article 4 asks whether charity's increase has a limit. In each person it actually stops at some point, but there is no limit beyond which it could not increase. Charity tends to infinite divine charity, and immaterial capacity is enlarged by what it receives, like the potential infinity of number. Christ's grace is qualifiedly infinite and cannot increase. The Virgin reached the summit of purity but grew in charity, and the blessed do not grow because they are at the end of the way.
claims: Charity's increase has no limit beyond which it could not go, since capacity grows with grace.

ta-l1d17q2-Dd1e3708.summary: Article 5 asks whether charity decreases. Thomas holds that it does not diminish essentially; it is lost only by mortal sin and can be reinfused in lesser degree. Its firmness comes from God, so cessation of acts cools only its fervour. Venial sin concerns means, not the end, and does not reach the summit of affection where charity clings to the end. It diminishes only rootedness and fervour and disposes to mortal sin.
claims: Charity does not decrease essentially; venial sin diminishes only its fervour and rootedness.

ta-l1d17q2-Dd1e3758.summary: The Expositio textus of the second part of Distinction 17 argues that God's greatness in us implies something created and judges Lombard's answers to the objections from authority insufficient. It explains the 'proper measure' of grace by predestination, capacity, and effort, and distinguishes the common gifts of sanctifying grace from freely given graces distributed for the Church.
claims: Lombard's replies leave unexplained how the Spirit causes love without a habit.

ta-l1d17q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 17 treats the increase and decrease of charity, pressing Thomas's case against Lombard's identification of charity with the Spirit. Article 1 holds that charity increases essentially, in quantity of power and intensity, by alteration broadly taken, which Lombard's view cannot explain. Article 2 holds that it grows not by addition but by intensification, as the infused act is brought from imperfect to perfect through the recipient's preparation, God infusing and increasing grace by one operation. Article 3 holds that an act of charity disposes for and merits increase, which follows immediately on an act from one's whole power. Charity's firmness comes from God, so one act can suffice. Article 4 holds that charity's increase has no limit in principle, since the soul's capacity grows with what it receives. Article 5 holds that charity does not decrease essentially: venial sin, concerning only means, reduces fervour and rootedness, and only mortal sin removes charity.
claims: Charity increases essentially by intensification, not addition, through the recipient's preparation.
An act of charity from one's whole power merits immediate increase.
Charity's increase has no limit in principle.
Charity does not decrease; venial sin affects only fervour, mortal sin removes charity.
